a tour of a giant blue screen stage. a miniature jungle with a model helicopter, a raptor on a rock pillar snapping it out of the air. a scale city with water pouring through it. a swamp set where a crocodile lunges at two actors on a rope bridge while the camera crew keeps rolling. it ends on a spinosaurus under stage lights with broken gear on the floor

a real practical effects shoot like this is a studio, a rig team and a budget most films never get. here it is a few stills and one model

to make one: one still per set, one shot per creature, cut them like a behind the scenes tour

would you have believed it was a real set if nobody told you?

one of the biggest obstacles in ai video is fine-grained control of what the actors do in a scene, and iterating on it.

blocking the scene out in blender, then running video-to-video with a reference image for the look, has been done before. but it made every iteration ten times slower

we’ve removed that barrier by hosting blender in the cloud. now you can have agents building different scenes side by side, nailing every small detail, with full control of sequencing and timing

Went to the film premiere of Luca Guadagnino's ‘Artificial’ (OpenAI movie) in SF tonight. 
Sharing notes on how the movie was made from the live Q&A with Luca and actors Andrew Garfield (Sam Altman), Monica Barbaro (Mira Murati) & Cooper Hoffman (Greg Brockman):

Luca’s Vision
-Luca: cinema is “like a lie that tells the truth”
-Luca: “It’s never about the object, it’s always about the people. It’s not about AGI or AI, it’s about the conflict between worldview and way of being”
-Core tension: Ilya’s idealism vs. the “brutality of the factual desire for prevailing”
-Luca describes it as a “Shakespearean feud” that led to Sam Altman’s ousting and return in 2023
-Andrew quoting Luca’s pitch: “this is a John Hughes movie. This is a high school screwball comedy, just with slightly higher stakes, mixed in with a little bit of Invasion of the Body Snatchers”

Shooting on and off location
-San Francisco - the city is a protagonist, mirroring the shift from utopia to dystopia
-Inspired by "Philadelphia" (film by Jonathan Demme) as a model for city-as-character
-Coit Tower frescoes cited as an emblem of the city’s original utopian promise
-Most corporate interiors built on a soundstage near Luca’s home in Italy (Luca acknowledged a budget constraint)

Playing Sam Altman
-Andrew on Sam Altman: Key image is Sam as a ninja in a video game, collecting amulets of power undetected. 
-“You’re not aware that he [Sam] is putting you in a cage and leaving the key on the inside of the cage”
-Sam’s gait and how he "perches": the seated posture (crisscross applesauce): “the way he [Sam] sat was tactical. Whether it’s conscious or not, again, is for us all to kind of debate”
-On Sam’s relationship to truth, Andrew cited mythologist Michael Meade: when power comes into a space, “it’s very hard for truth to remain in that space as well”
-Andrew playing Sam internally: “everything I say is for a greater purpose”
-The Vanity Fair incident: Sam said on camera “we waved at each other”; Luca confirmed neither he nor Andrew was present for it

Playing Mira Murati & Greg Brockman
-Monica on Mira Murati: “Intensely private,” which limited research but revealed character. 
-Mira grew up in communist Albania where education “was a kid’s sort of currency”
-“She’s kind of always been a fish out of water”: young, a woman in tech, an immigrant
-Mira and Ilya’s bond rooted in shared outsider status and idealism
-Greg Brockman wedding anecdote: married at the OpenAI offices, Ilya officiated, a robot was the ring bearer. (but they didn't film this scene unfort)

Filming the ChatGPT Breakthrough Scene (where it successfully beats a human player in a video game)
-Luca’s approach: “freeze the moment instead of trim the moment”
-Luca’s direction for the scene: “Put them in underwear”
-Shot slowmo at 2,000 frames per second, “very few shots, like 2”
-Background cast celebrating in slow motion; Sam and Ilya kept in real time. -This was a visual device to show they alone understood the magnitude of what was unleashed.
-Andrew and Cooper practiced outside between setups in tighty-whities, spraying soda cans and champagne bottles
-Limited takes because getting wet meant having to dry off and reset
-Monica watched from the sidelines and described the intimate Andrew/Yura moment: “like they had just given birth to this new creation that they understood better than anyone else in the world how drastically this was going to change the face of humanity”.

THIS IS F**KING WILD.

none of this is real btw. no actors, no set, no camera. the whole scene is AI

the faces, the snow, the light on the satin, even the timing of the joke… a year ago AI video couldn't land a punchline. now it's doing christmas rom-com better than half of netflix

honestly the wild part isn't the quality. i watched it twice before it even hit me that it's fake

would you have noticed?

AI can now build a 3D world in minutes, and it looks stunning. then you step inside, and nothing moves. 

the lid stays shut, the character stands frozen, and all you can do is look. we call it the dead scene, and it's the biggest gap in AI 3D today.

Manycore's Aholo stack already holds the cure. 

SpatialGen generates the world, and Lux3D makes the object, splits it into real parts, gives it joints, and rigs a character

but each of those is a separate tool with a separate result, and nobody had put them in one room.

so I built Holorra for the @ManycoreTech Aholo Global 3D AI Hackathon: one browser tab where all of it becomes a single scene you can play. 

Generate the world, split the parts, rig the actors, direct the scene.

everything in it is real. 

an espresso machine came from one sentence, was cut into 4 parts without losing a single triangle, and got a working hinge and drawer from one more sentence. 

the actor began as a statue, then got 52 joints in 81 seconds and 8 moves in 17. 

you press Play, walk her through a Gaussian splat room, collect the beans, brew the coffee, frame the shot and dance.

it runs on a phone, the co-director takes orders in English or Chinese, and you need no key and no sign-up.

check it out: https://holorra.xyz/

Built on the full Aholo stack, with thanks to @Aholo_Lux3D and Manycore.

#Manycorehackathon #AholoLux3D #AIHackathon

Upcoming PALWORLD VIDEO TEASER 

THEOLOGICAL POST ABOUT AI 
(Be open minded, I care not for tribalism biases. This will be my first time expressing my thoughts on this platform with no sarcasm/condescending/mockery tone):

The thing about creating is that the tool we use will always have it's own limit attributed to how capable its user is. 

A pencil on the hands of a highschooler isn't creating the same craft of the man who has experience. The same applies with being an actor and AI.

Actors and AI are specially tied together because they both are vessels of a larger thing, hence why I am drawing the parallels for all Anti-AI people to understand.

An actor can be great and can even improvise on his own, but the scene structure, the lighting, the ambient, the scenery and setting itself, the lines of script, the expression and feelings conveyed by the actor?
All of these were the filmmaker's vision. The actor is a conduit to this.

The same way a pencil is but a conduit or AI is but a conduit too.

This is why when people say that AI will replace things, I laugh at it.

Because the theological idea that, at some point, artificial intelligence is capable of generating human emotion to the finest detail, means that it would be the perfect conduit that would work way faster than any actor/pen would.

But this is not a loss of humanity's sense of uniqueness. You don't need to be scared for the lack of sense of purpose or "soul" that we all have that somehow is being replaced. No.

We still are superior to any other species on the Universe. You are just looking at it from a different, emotional perspective.

So allow me to bring up a new perspective that you should agree with about Humanity :

Tools are made for a reason. We innovate on them because we always ask "What if?"

A human, 400,000 years ago, looked at the sparks of flint and stone, and created fire for the first time, and then said "What if?" and used said fire to cook food and use it to attack other living beings.

A human asked themselves "What if?" when they looked at birds for millenia, envy to the idea of flight, until we ourselves created the very first mechanical bird wings, which then, from the Wright Brothers, came the very first plane.

We've always been using our vision since the dawn of time to ask ourselves "What if?".

That's what we do when we create stories too via art, books and movies. It being Jurassic Park, Star Wars or even Mona Lisa.

It is not the tool or how it is interpreted that makes it humane, it is the lived experience, the love, the loss, the happiness and sadness that made each and every single one of us humans different from each other.

And this is why Vision will always exist, because to be human is to have vision and to Create with that vision.

Artists jobs may be lost. (The conduits for art).
Actor jobs may be lost. (The conduits for cinematography).
But we will always be able to Create, no matter how advanced AI gets, because AI is just a superhuman conduit, that needs its pilot.

We had this specifically whenever we decided to create the first car, when carriage makers and blacksmiths lost their jobs and had to adapt, probably becoming mechanics now.

We had automation that clearly does the production job way better than manufacture too, which also led to the loss of many people's jobs too.

To create, is to innovate.
And those things are not tied to jobs of the past.
Hence why humanity learns to adapt, learn how to use Televisions, cell phones, computers.

Innovation through creation will always lead to the loss of certain jobs of the past, but that doesn't make humanity lose its purpose, it's uniqueness...

It's.... Soul.

Perhaps the daunting feeling of what could be the meaning of life was always there - right in front of us - ever since we were born.

Perhaps the meaning of life is, like God who created the Universe, be our own agents in creating our own mini-Universes that we have in our minds.

Our own visions to create.

Creating will always be part of what makes us humans, 
and that's what makes us different from other species.

Regardless if now we have an ultra-advanced vessel to interpret our visions instead of ink, we will always have that thing that makes us human.

Our visions to create.
And to create is to innovate.
Which is bound to lead to jobs of the past adapting or just being erased.

Food for thought.
